correctness.rationale: For m>=2, equality of polynomial squared moduli on an open t interval becomes a polynomial identity. A nonconstant rational quotient r=q/p with unimodular leading ratio has first Laurent deviation a z^(-k). Inserting u=t+iP(t), v=t-iP(t), its leading real part either survives at order P^(-k), or is purely imaginary, in which case the first displacement term is nonzero at order t P^(-k-1) and dominates all higher terms because t/|P(t)| tends to zero. Therefore r is constant. For the polynomial restriction map U->t+iP(t), V->t-iP(t), the principal ideal is generated by U-V-2iP((U+V)/2), of separate degrees (m,m). Multiplication respects degrees separately, so the bidegree-d kernel is a square of dimension max(d-m+1,0)^2. Hermitian fixed points and polarization give the real intensity dimension. Analytic independence ensures generic D-node full-profile interpolation on every interval, while rank-two absence and compactness give qualitative fixed-node inverse stability. A reflection across an affine line gives genuine degree-one ambiguity when m<=1. Finite exact modular checks corroborate only the rank and node claims.

value.rationale: The theorem solves a natural design question for all real polynomial measurement graphs, separating the exactly ambiguous affine case from every nonlinear case and giving the exact span dimension D_(m,d) for arbitrary degree pairs. It quantifies the transition from injective full Hermitian lifting to phase-only uniqueness, and gives sharp generic linear full-profile sampling on every arbitrarily short arc. It is an infinite family of natural measurement geometries, not a small numerical example or a renamed textbook lemma; the standard algebraic tools are not themselves claimed novel.
residual_risks: Finite-dimensional full-profile sample optimality is not a nonlinear optimality theorem.
Generic designs need not be uniformly well-conditioned; only a fixed-design positive lower bound is obtained.
